Write the introduction to a guide for a REST API that manages calendar bookings. Around 200 words.

# Introduction

The Bookings API gives your application programmatic control over a shared calendar: creating appointments, moving them, cancelling them, and asking what times are still open.

Every request goes over HTTPS to `https://api.example.com/v1`, authenticated with a bearer token you generate in the dashboard. Responses are JSON. Timestamps are RFC 3339 with an explicit offset, and each calendar carries an IANA timezone so recurring bookings survive daylight-saving shifts.

Four resources do most of the work. A *calendar* owns a set of working hours and a timezone. An *availability* query returns the free slots inside a window. A *booking* reserves one of those slots for a named attendee. A *hold* reserves a slot for a short period while a customer finishes checkout, and expires on its own if they never do.

Double-booking is the problem this API exists to prevent, so writes are conflict-checked at the calendar level. If two clients request the same slot, the second gets a 409 with the conflicting booking's ID. Send an `Idempotency-Key` header on writes and a retried request returns the original result instead of a duplicate.

The next section walks through issuing a key and making your first booking. Later sections cover recurrence rules, webhooks, and rate limits.

## Authentication

Every request carries a bearer token in the `Authorization` header: `Authorization: Bearer sk_live_...`. Generate tokens under Settings → API Keys in the dashboard, where each one is scoped to a single workspace and to a set of permissions (`calendars:read`, `bookings:write`, and so on). A token requesting an endpoint outside its scopes gets a 403 naming the missing scope. Keys are shown once at creation; if you lose one, revoke it and issue a replacement. Keep them on your server, since a browser-side key exposes every calendar in the workspace to anyone who opens the network tab. For customer-facing booking widgets, mint a short-lived client token from your backend with the `POST /v1/client_tokens` endpoint; those expire after 15 minutes and can only read availability and create holds. Requests without a valid token return 401 with an `error.code` of `unauthenticated`, and revoked keys stop working within a few seconds of revocation. Rotate keys by creating the new one, deploying it, then revoking the old one, since both stay valid in the meantime.
